code_triggers_common.text: Model IFC: approved coverage in all new buildings (IFC 2018 510.1), with exceptions; IFC 2024 adds Exception 4 for one-story buildings up to 12,000 sq ft with no below-ground area. Existing buildings: when a wired system cannot be repaired or is replaced, or within a time frame the adopting authority sets (1103.2). State carve-outs: Florida exempts 1-2 family, townhouses, buildings under 12,000 sq ft with no below-grade area, apartments/lodging under 3 storeys with exterior egress, and wood-frame apartments of 75 ft or less with under 150 units; and from 12/31/2026 requires no ERCES where exterior DAQ is below 3.4. North Carolina (SL 2025-50, 2 Jul 2025) exempts R-2 Type V apartments and apartments/hotels of 2 storeys or less with exterior egress, and lets existing systems there be disconnected. Minnesota requires coverage only where a local ordinance adopts Appendix P (Minn. R. 7511.0510, 7511.7900; Appendix Q is proposed for the 2024-based code, not adopted). Virginia makes the locality responsible for the acceptance test (13VAC5-63-240, 918.1.1).

value_beyond_code.item: Cellular coverage for tenants and visitors
value_beyond_code.claim: Owners now carry indoor cellular themselves: WIA experts describe an industry-wide 'carrier no' posture toward broadly funded in-building builds, and 'carriers are increasingly reluctant to fund in-building systems'.
CommScope/Coleman Parkes (2016) estimated only about 2% of commercial buildings have dedicated technology for strong indoor mobile coverage and capacity. Survey estimate, 2016.

Measured (Ookla indoor readings + CoStar): large Grade A London offices with reliable indoor mobile coverage ask about 10% more rent than poor-coverage peers after local peer adjustment; no consistent gap in Grade B. UK data; US effect not measured.

Same study: within three years about 16% of space in the worst-connected large Grade A buildings reaches a lease event vs under 2% in the best-connected (exposure to lease events, not measured move-outs).
Estimates only: building professionals surveyed for CommScope (2016) put the value uplift at 28% on average; a Nextivity executive (WIA, 2026) says a 5-10% premium is possible.

The FCC (2025) restates that consumers keep replacing landlines with wireless phones and 'a majority of wireless calls are now made indoors'; cellular coverage indoors is where occupants' 911 calls start.

value_beyond_code.item: Responder broadband (FirstNet Band 14) and code scope
value_beyond_code.claim: Public safety names in-building coverage a top FirstNet priority; IFC 2024 510.4.1.1 measures DAQ on 'narrowband analog, digital or wideband LTE signals'; NFPA 1225 A.18.6.1 says carrying a commercial broadband signal needs that licensee's prior approval. FirstNet's authority lapses 22 Feb 2027 unless reauthorized.

ERCES compliance falls on the owner; FCC forfeitures can exceed $100,000 per continuing violation; late discovery can move the ribbon-cutting months; San Diego holds the TCO until the ERCES is permitted, installed and tested. The FCC finds rogue boosters by direction finding and sends Notifications of Harmful Interference with a 10-day reply: Hallandale Beach FL, 13 May 2025 (a Class A Axell booster in 799-805 MHz hitting Broward's 800 MHz system), and a Texas apartment, April 2025 (858-859 MHz, no consent). APCO's 2024 survey: 53.7% of 41 licensees have had booster noise or interference.

Hospitals: 75% use smartphones as the main communication tool and 39% still call cellular coverage a challenge (Spok 2019, 450+ respondents). Building pros surveyed for CommScope cited workforce productivity (77%) and recruiting (46%).
Venue neutral-host DAS is sized for tens of thousands of devices at once (Extenet); 39% of building pros surveyed cited attracting more visitors.
Current DAS platforms carry cellular IoT (ANDREW ERA lists LTE Cat-M1 and NB-IoT); integrators run IoT on the same fiber backbone as cellular and Wi-Fi (Airwavz); Nextivity sells IoT sensor networks.

CBRS is 3550-3700 MHz; General Authorized Access users may operate across the band (47 CFR 96.11). OEMs sell private-network platforms (JMA private wireless, Nextivity WAVE CBRS NaaS); ADRF expects broader private 5G adoption.
Third-party neutral hosts can fund, build and run the DAS, with recurring revenue often shared with the venue at an agreed rate; other models are venue-funded or a monthly managed fee (NaaS).
Reserving pathways, riser space, power and wall space early costs far less than retrofitting after finishes; reserved space can be reused if no ERCES is needed.

process.what: Confirm which code edition and local amendment the AHJ enforces, the frequency license holder, and the construction stage.
process.customer_provides: Address, occupancy, floors above/below grade, square footage, construction schedule, AHJ contact if known.

process.phase: Site walk / RF survey (benchmark grid test)
process.what: Measure public safety signal into and out of the building on the AHJ's grid (20 areas per floor, center of each) and donor signal at the roof; for new builds, a baseline assessment first and detailed measurements once the building is closed in.
process.duration: 1-3 days on site for a typical building (estimate)
process.customer_provides: Access to every floor incl. stairs, elevators, roof and basements; escort; floor plans.

process.what: Predictive coverage maps, donor link budget, isolation calculations, riser and cable diagrams, backup power calculations, FACU monitoring design, test grids; preliminary, updated and final designs. SBC: an ERCES design cannot be finalized until the building is substantially complete.
process.duration: A few weeks for a standard enterprise building; several months for airports/stadiums (CTS)
process.customer_provides: CAD/PDF floor plans and elevations, construction type per floor, riser and pathway locations.

process.what: Design goes to the frequency license holder (often the county radio shop) with a retransmission authorization; non-licensee operation needs the licensee's express consent kept in a recordable form.
process.duration: Not published. Terms are: Douglas Co. provisional 6 months then 5 years (search excerpt); MD FiRST provisional 1 year, then final after a de-sense test; Broward and Fairfax renew annually; PSERN validates the uplink before activation (search excerpt). Proposed FCC framework (RM-12009): 3-year terms.
process.customer_provides: Owner signature on retransmission authorization / agreement.

process.what: Construction permit for the ERCES; in Fairfax: radio shop approval, then building permit (fire-rated penetrations), low-voltage permit and fire alarm permit, in that order.
process.duration: 2-6 weeks per review cycle (estimate; Fairfax and San Diego publish no review times)
process.customer_provides: Owner authorization, permit fees, fire alarm contractor coordination.

process.what: Each carrier reviews the design and provides or approves a signal source; carrier-direct sources are not guaranteed.
process.duration: Carrier-direct timelines can run 12 to 24 months per carrier with no guaranteed outcome (CTS)
process.customer_provides: Carrier relationships, signed agreements, rack space for carrier equipment.

process.what: UL 2524-listed active equipment (IFC 2021 and 2024; NFPA 1225 18.12.1.3); prefer 3rd-edition listings (UL 2524:2024; Intertek withdraws un-updated listings after 2026-03-22). NEMA Type 4 cabinets for boosters, NEMA 3R battery cabinets, cable and passives.
Donor antenna and surge protection, headend/BDA, backbone and distribution cabling, antennas, power, FACU interface; pathway survivability where required.
process.duration: Weeks for a mid-size building (estimate); CTS says a few months to deploy for standard enterprise DAS
process.customer_provides: Roof and riser access, dedicated power and generator connection, ceiling access, firestop coordination.

process.what: Set gains, filters and AGC; isolation test; check for oscillation with a spectrum analyzer; BDA commissioning tests (e.g., PCTEL BDA suite).

Grid test to 95% two-way coverage per floor (20 areas; up to 40 if two fail); San Diego requires a third-party tester (FCC GROL + NICET IB-PSC Level II) not related to the installer and an SDFD inspection before TCO; Fairfax: radio shop first, then fire alarm, building and coverage inspections.
process.customer_provides: Building access, radios or loaner radios coordinated with the agency.

process.what: Register Class B signal booster installations in the FCC signal booster database; SBC lists this as part of acceptance.
process.customer_provides: Owner/operator contact details for the registration.

process.what: Acceptance documentation (equipment list, data sheets, as-builts, measurements, power calcs, frequencies, isolation results, settings); San Diego returns a stamped report that is uploaded to The Compliance Engine, starting the annual cycle.
process.customer_provides: Place to keep originals; on-site document holder at the BDA.

process.what: Supervisory signals to a listed fire alarm control unit (AC loss, charger failure, donor antenna, active device failure, low battery at 70%, link to FACU); commercial DAS often adds 24/7 NOC monitoring.
process.customer_provides: FACU points and central station account.

process.what: Test, document and sign by an AHJ-approved person at acceptance and every 12 months: coverage test, gain check, 1-hour battery load test, active components; report to the fire code official. NFPA 1225 20.3.10.2.3.3 (per SBC): full quantitative retest at least every five years; the IFC has no 5-year rule (vendors who cite IFC 510.6 for it are wrong). IFC 2024 510.6.1 also requires a retest after additions or remodels. NYC ARCS: daily console check, annual certification, 5-year recertification. San Diego adds semiannual visual inspections; Fairfax requires annual re-submission of retransmission authorization.
process.customer_provides: Maintenance agreement, access, prior test report and gain values.

supply_or_decide.detail: Site plan, floor plans for every level incl. ones the system does not cover, elevations, construction type per floor; San Diego wants graduated scale and compass on sheets.
Every floor, stairs, elevators, roof, basements; agency staff may enter at any reasonable time for field testing, and San Diego requires 24/7 access to investigate interference.
Donor antenna mounting, line of sight to the agency site, isolation from inside antennas (20 dB above system gain), discharge units on donor coax.
12 hours at 100% from dedicated battery, or 2-hour battery plus generator that can carry the load for 12 hours.
Riser design shown on building plans with listed firestop systems for penetrations; pathway survivability per design.
Full ERCES needs a fire alarm permit showing ERCES signals monitored by the FACU.
Commercial DAS and private networks share fiber backbone and may need network ports for NOC monitoring; public safety supervision goes to the FACU, not IT.
Owner pays for code-required ERCES and later frequency changes; site assessment usually comes before a budget can be set.
Commercial DAS needs each carrier's approval and a signal source; owners cannot assume a carrier will fund one.
Retransmission authorization / annual testing-maintenance-retransmission agreement (Fairfax) and licensee consent records.

objections.objection: Our radios already work in here.
objections.answer: Then prove it: San Diego accepts a Proof of Acceptable Coverage grid test instead of a system; if coverage passes, no ERCES is needed.

objections.objection: The carriers will pay for it.
objections.answer: Not for most buildings now: carrier-direct timelines run 12-24 months per carrier with no guarantee, and WIA experts report carriers pulling back from funding.

objections.objection: The fire marshal approved it, so we can switch it on.
objections.answer: The frequency license holder must also approve the design, and a non-licensee needs the licensee's express consent before operating a booster.

objections.objection: We will deal with it after we open.
objections.answer: San Diego will not release a TCO until the ERCES is permitted, installed and tested; SBC: late discovery moves the opening months.

objections.objection: Why pay for a test every year?
objections.answer: Code: tested at acceptance and every 12 months, with a report to the fire code official; lost gain records force a rerun of the acceptance test.

objections.objection: Can one system do cellular and public safety?
objections.answer: Platforms exist that carry both (ANDREW ERA, Airwavz); some AHJs require a public safety dedicated ERCES, so check the local standard first.

It can: licensees must fix interference, operation may be ordered to stop, and non-public-safety amplifiers that degrade the ERCES must be corrected or removed. Design and commissioning tests exist to prevent this.

objections.objection: Can we just buy a cell booster off the shelf?
objections.answer: A consumer booster needs the subscriber's carrier consent and registration; an industrial booster (labelled NOT a CONSUMER device, for FCC licensees and qualified installers) needs a licence or the licensees' express consent.

Codes and SBC give none. Integrators publish their own ranges per sq ft installed: $0.50-2.50 (The Network Installers, 2026), $0.65-2.50 (MetroWireless, 2025), $0.50-2.00 and up (ERCES.co) (retrofit 2-3x; small buildings cost more per foot because the BDA and donor are fixed), roughly $50k to over $500k a job, and $2,500-15,000 a year for the annual test. All vendor figures, not independent surveys. Early pathways and a sprinklered building (no 2-h backbone, NFPA 1225 18.12.3.3) are the cheapest levers.

deliverables.line: All equipment locations; AHJ may require as-built design documents in its format.
Measurements at all covered locations, isolation results, measured signal source levels, all channel/gain/filter/AGC settings, signed by an AHJ-approved person.
All system equipment and manufacturer data sheets in the acceptance package.
Amplifier gain values kept on file with the owner for annual comparison.
Stamped/approved report and inspection sign-off (San Diego: stamped report uploaded to The Compliance Engine).
Written consent of the frequency licensee in a recordable form; Fairfax retransmission agreement renewed annually.
Class B booster installation registered in the FCC signal booster database.
Approved plans, latest annual report, authorization to operate, maintenance log at the BDA/BBU (San Diego).
Supervisory signals on the fire alarm panel; commercial DAS may add NOC monitoring.
Maintenance agreement for monitoring and periodic testing; annual test schedule.
Equipment and workmanship warranty terms are set by the maker and integrator; no code requirement found (estimate).

compare_dimensions.buyer_asks: How fast can you get through the AHJ and licensee?
compare_dimensions.rf_recon_firm_shows: FCC data pre-survey and link budget before the site walk, so the first submittal has donor path and isolation numbers the AHJ asks for.

compare_dimensions.buyer_asks: Will the report pass first time?
compare_dimensions.rf_recon_firm_shows: Grid test and AHJ report laid out to the 20-area grid, 95% rule and DAQ fields the code names.

compare_dimensions.buyer_asks: What do we keep for the fire marshal and annual tests?
compare_dimensions.rf_recon_firm_shows: Spec sheet packets and the acceptance-document list (equipment, data sheets, settings) assembled from the BOM.
Consent letters drafted for the licensee, as 90.219 requires.

compare_dimensions.buyer_asks: Capex, NaaS, or neutral-host revenue share?
compare_dimensions.rf_recon_firm_shows: Supplier quotes attached to the bid so the price is itemized; no claim on financing.

prospect_types.why: New construction under 510.1. Texas 19 TAC 103.1215 requires school systems to ensure law enforcement and emergency responder two-way radios operate effectively within each instructional facility. Michigan HB 5561 (introduced 2021; status not checked) would require ERRC in school buildings.
prospect_types.owner_why: Solid walls, stairwells and basements are where radios lose signal, and in a school that's where responders may need them most.
prospect_types.decision_maker: District facilities director / director of safety and security (estimate)

prospect_types.why: Many buildings, often over local size triggers (e.g., Seattle 50,000 sq ft total area, San Diego 20,000 sq ft or 3+ stories); campus-wide cellular and private networks.
prospect_types.owner_why: Campus buildings vary in age and construction, and radio signals can fade inside the larger ones.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Director of facilities / campus IT / campus fire marshal (estimate)

prospect_types.why: Large, often below grade; 39% of Spok's healthcare respondents still call cellular coverage a challenge; Fairfax's owner statement commits to maintenance per NFPA and Joint Commission standards.
prospect_types.owner_why: Hospitals are large and often have floors below ground, where radio signals fade.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Director of facilities / plant operations; IT telecom manager (estimate)

prospect_types.why: High-rise is a direct trigger in local amendments (Seattle, Nevada: floor more than 55 ft above lowest fire department access; San Diego: all new high-rises must have an ERCES; existing high-rises without phone-jack systems must test and install within 3 years if they fail). Leasing value from cellular coverage.
prospect_types.owner_why: Upper floors, stairwells and core areas are where radio signals often fall short in tall buildings.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Property manager / chief engineer; asset manager for cellular (estimate)

prospect_types.why: Large single-story floor plates exceed local area triggers (Seattle 50,000 sq ft; San Diego 20,000 sq ft); IFC 2024 one-story exemption stops at 12,000 sq ft.
prospect_types.owner_why: Large floor areas and full racking can block radio signals well inside the building.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Developer / GC project manager during construction; facilities manager (estimate)

prospect_types.why: Below-grade triggers: Nevada (any floor below the lowest exit discharge), Seattle (occupied floors 30+ ft below exit discharge, basements 10,000+ sq ft), San Diego (basement over 2,500 sq ft).
prospect_types.owner_why: Levels below ground are where radio signals are weakest.

prospect_types.why: Size triggers plus shopper cellular demand; neutral-host revenue share possible.
prospect_types.owner_why: Large floor areas and interior stores can leave radio signals weak deep inside the building.

prospect_types.why: Large assembly occupancy; neutral-host DAS for tens of thousands of devices; usually served by national neutral hosts.
prospect_types.owner_why: Concrete concourses and service levels are where radio signals often fall short.

prospect_types.why: Size triggers and peak cellular load; neutral-host market.
prospect_types.owner_why: Large halls and service areas can leave radio signals weak well inside the building.

prospect_types.why: Large footprint and below-grade areas; vendors pitch one platform for public cellular, private networks, IoT and public safety.
prospect_types.owner_why: Long concourses, service levels and areas below ground are where radio signals often fall short.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Airport IT / telecom manager; airport fire marshal (estimate)

prospect_types.why: High-rise and size triggers; guest cellular expectations.
prospect_types.owner_why: Stairwells, corridors and back-of-house areas are where radio signals often fall short.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Chief engineer / director of engineering; GM (estimate)

prospect_types.why: Very large floor plates and concrete; Extenet runs neutral-host DAS for Las Vegas resort and convention properties.
prospect_types.owner_why: Very large floors and heavy construction can leave radio signals weak well inside the building.

prospect_types.why: New construction under 510.1; FirstNet in-building focus on police HQs, fire stations and 911 centers.
prospect_types.owner_why: Heavy construction and floors below ground can leave radio signals weak inside.

prospect_types.why: Below-grade triggers; Boldyn cites a deployment 173 ft under New York City.
prospect_types.owner_why: Platforms and tunnels below ground are where radio signals are weakest.

prospect_types.why: I-2 healthcare occupancy with life-safety-sensitive owners; CMS lists 14,686 facilities with their own coordinates, certified beds, ownership, chain and whether automatic sprinklers cover all required areas (2026-11-04 data scout).
prospect_types.owner_why: Long corridors and solid walls can weaken radio signals, and residents depend on a fast response.
prospect_types.decision_maker: Facility administrator or director of maintenance; the chain's facilities lead where one owns it (estimate: not in the research)

prospect_types.why: Road tunnels (NFPA 502) and rail and transit tunnels (NFPA 130) call for emergency responder radio inside; the owner is a public agency or a railroad, so one owner can have several. Found from OpenStreetMap per area (ODbL).
prospect_types.owner_why: Radio signals don't reach far underground without help.
prospect_types.decision_maker: The owner's tunnel or systems engineer: state DOT, toll or transit authority, railroad (estimate: not in the research)

prospect_sources.name: NCES Common Core of Data (CCD) school directory
prospect_sources.format: ZIP with CSV and SAS (13.4 MB zip; 41 MB CSV)
prospect_sources.coverage: All US public schools; 102,178 rows in SY 2024-25 v1a (98,507 operating)
prospect_sources.fields: SCH_NAME, LEA_NAME, mailing and location address, PHONE (filled on all rows), WEBSITE (70,314 rows filled), NCESSCH, SCH_TYPE, CHARTER, grades, LEVEL. No lat/lon (join EDGE by NCESSCH); no enrollment (separate membership file).
prospect_sources.terms: US government work, public domain in the US (17 USC 105); open data may be used for any purpose, commercial or not. The NCES pages read carry no separate terms.

prospect_sources.name: NCES EDGE public school locations
prospect_sources.format: Zipped shapefile (29 MB); ArcGIS web service
prospect_sources.fields: NCESSCH, NAME, STREET, CITY, STATE, ZIP, LAT, LON, LOCALE, county, CBSA
prospect_sources.terms: Hub record points to resources.data.gov open licenses (US government work, public domain).

prospect_sources.name: NCES Private School Universe Survey (PSS)
prospect_sources.fields: PINST (name), PADDRS, PCITY, PSTABB, PZIP, PPHONE, LATITUDE24, LONGITUDE24, NUMSTUDS (enrollment); 359 columns
prospect_sources.terms: US government work, public domain; no separate terms on the page.

prospect_sources.name: IPEDS institutional directory (HD)
prospect_sources.fields: INSTNM, ADDR, CITY, STABBR, ZIP, CHFNM and CHFTITLE (chief administrator name and title), GENTELE (phone), WEBADDR, LATITUDE, LONGITUD, SECTOR, CONTROL, HOSPITAL, MEDICAL, INSTSIZE, Carnegie size

prospect_sources.name: CMS Hospital General Information
prospect_sources.fields: Facility ID, name, address, city, state, ZIP, county, Telephone Number, Hospital Type, Ownership, Emergency Services, overall rating. No lat/lon, no bed count.
prospect_sources.terms: Metastore record carries no licence field; CMS says its public data products are freely available; US government work (17 USC 105).

prospect_sources.name: HIFLD Open (hospitals, sport venues, etc.)
prospect_sources.terms: HIFLD Open is decommissioned (portal closed Aug 26, 2025); many layers moved behind HIFLD Secure or back to source agencies.
prospect_sources.commercial_or_marketing_restriction: Not usable as a live source

prospect_sources.name: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API
prospect_sources.fields: Tags such as amenity=school/hospital/university, shop=mall, amenity=parking + parking=multi-storey/underground (capacity), tourism=hotel, leisure=stadium; name, phone, website, operator where mapped; building:levels, height.
prospect_sources.terms: ODbL: free to copy, distribute and adapt with credit to OpenStreetMap contributors; altered data may be distributed only under the same licence. Public Overpass: under 10,000 queries and 1 GB a day; commercial use should use self-hosted or paid Overpass servers.
prospect_sources.commercial_or_marketing_restriction: Commercial use allowed under ODbL with attribution and share-alike; public Overpass server asks commercial users to self-host or pay.

prospect_sources.name: Overture Maps Places
prospect_sources.coverage: Global; about 88 million records (about 60 million from Meta, 16 million from BrightQuery)
prospect_sources.fields: names, basic_category, taxonomy, websites, phones, emails, socials, addresses, confidence, brand
prospect_sources.terms: Per-source licences: CDLA Permissive 2.0 (Meta, Microsoft and others), Apache 2.0 (Foursquare, keep NOTICE), CC0 (AllThePlaces). No OSM data in Places. Overture warns of duplicates, high junk rate and low completeness.
prospect_sources.commercial_or_marketing_restriction: None stated on the attribution page

prospect_sources.name: FAA airports (ADDS)
prospect_sources.coverage: 19,558 charted airports (US, PR, VI, some border facilities)
prospect_sources.fields: IDENT, ICAO_ID, NAME, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE, TYPE_CODE, SERVCITY, STATE, OPERSTATUS, PRIVATEUSE
prospect_sources.terms: Custom licence text: 'The data provided is for public use'; not an official source for non-US airports.

prospect_sources.name: FEMA USA Structures
prospect_sources.coverage: 146,381,550 structures over 450 sq ft, US and territories
prospect_sources.fields: OCC_CLS (e.g., Commercial, Education, Government, Industrial, Assembly), PRIM_OCC, SQFEET, HEIGHT (only for NGA 133-city LiDAR), LATITUDE/LONGITUDE, FIPS. No names or contacts.

prospect_sources.name: Microsoft US Building Footprints
prospect_sources.download: Per-state GeoJSON zips linked from the repo
prospect_sources.fields: Footprint polygon, capture date where known; no height, no names

prospect_sources.name: Census County Business Patterns
prospect_sources.coverage: Establishment counts, employment and payroll by industry and size class, by county and ZIP
prospect_sources.fields: Counts only; no business names (disclosure avoidance)

prospect_sources.name: City building permit data (example: Chicago Building Permits)
prospect_sources.fields: PERMIT_TYPE, WORK_DESCRIPTION, address, LATITUDE/LONGITUDE, REPORTED_COST, CONTACT_1..15_NAME and type (contractors, owners)
prospect_sources.terms: Licence field says 'See Terms of Use'; the chicago.gov terms page returned 403, so not read.
prospect_sources.commercial_or_marketing_restriction: UNVERIFIED - read the city's terms before marketing use

prospect_sources.name: CMS Nursing Home Provider Information
prospect_sources.download: Named by the metastore (https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/api/1/metastore/schemas/dataset/items/4pq5-n9py); Oct 2026: NH_ProviderInfo_Oct2026.csv
prospect_sources.coverage: 14,686 Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes (datastore count, 2026-11-04)
prospect_sources.fields: CCN, provider name, address, city, state, ZIP, phone, ownership type, certified beds, chain, in-hospital flag, automatic sprinklers in all required areas, latitude, longitude
prospect_sources.terms: The same CMS public data terms as the hospital list: the metastore carries no licence field and access level public; CMS says its public data products are freely available; US government work (17 USC 105).

outreach_rules.detail: No exception for business-to-business email; applies to any message whose primary purpose is commercial.
From, To, Reply-To and routing must identify the sender; subject must reflect the content. Send from a real, named person at the firm.
Clearly disclose the message is an advertisement (format is flexible).
Include a valid physical postal address.
Clear way to stop all marketing email; must work at least 30 days after sending; honour within 10 business days; no fee or extra data to opt out.
Hiring a sender does not move responsibility; penalties up to $53,088 per violating email.
All senders: SPF or DKIM, valid forward/reverse DNS, TLS, spam rate under 0.3% (aim under 0.1%). Over 5,000/day to Gmail: SPF + DKIM + DMARC, From alignment, one-click unsubscribe.

outreach_rules.rule: TCPA: autodialed or prerecorded calls/texts to cell phones
outreach_rules.detail: Need prior express consent; telemarketing ones need prior express written consent. Hand-dialed calls are outside (a)(1).
National DNC protects residential subscribers; honour company-specific do-not-call requests within 10 business days and keep them 5 years; residential calls only 8 am-9 pm local.

outreach_rules.rule: FTC Telemarketing Sales Rule B2B exemption
outreach_rules.detail: Calls between a telemarketer and a business are exempt except 310.3(a)(2) and (4); calls selling nondurable office or cleaning supplies are not exempt.
One first email plus one follow-up about a week later, then stop unless they reply; a call only by hand-dial to a business line (estimate; house norm, no legal source).
